extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors, curriculum designers, and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative dimensions for undergraduate mathematics instruction and for analyzing mathematical thinking (a framework for research and pedagogy). Emphasizes instructional goals, classroom design as communities of practice, and cognitive components relevant to problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide students a sense of the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should provide students with a sense of the discipline -- a sense of its scope, power, uses, and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conveys that courses should situate mathematics within its broader context (historical development, applicability, and intellectual reach) so students appreciate what the field is about rather than only isolated techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give students a sense of what mathematics is and how it is done; foster value and confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It should give them a sense of what mathematics is and how it is done, at a level appropriate for the students to experience and understand. As a result of their instructional experiences, students should learn to value mathematics and to feel confident in their ability to do mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should expose students to authentic mathematical activity at an appropriate depth so they develop appreciation and self-efficacy in doing mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop understanding of important concepts in core content
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should develop students' understanding of important concepts in the appropriate core content (see Curriculum Recommendations from the MAA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize key conceptual ideas from the curriculum rather than only peripheral facts; align teaching with recognized core recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at conceptual understanding rather than mere mechanical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should be aimed at conceptual understanding rather than at mere mechanical skills, and at developing in students the ability to apply the subject matter they have studied with flexibility and resourcefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sense-making, connections, and transfer; avoid curricula that focus only on rote procedures without understanding or adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities to explore a broad range of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should provide students the opportunity to explore a broad range of problems and problem situations, ranging from exercises to open-ended problems and exploratory situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include routine practice, structured exercises, open-ended tasks, and exploratory investigations so students experience multiple problem types and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a broad range of approaches and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: It should provide students with a broad range of approaches and techniques (ranging from the straightforward application of the appropriate algorithmic methods to the use of approximation methods, various modeling techniques, and the use of heuristic problem solving strategies) for dealing with such problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach algorithmic methods alongside approximation, modeling, heuristics, and heuristic strategies so students can choose appropriate tools for different problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help students develop a mathematical point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should help students to develop what might be called a 'mathematical point of view' -- a predilection to analyze and understand, to perceive structure and structural relationships, to see how things fit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate habits of looking for structure, relationships, and unifying perspectives; this is part of enculturation into mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop analytical skills and ability to reason in extended chains
rubrics_metrics.description: It should help students develop their analytical skills, and the ability to reason in extended chains of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and scaffolding that require multi-step reasoning and support students in constructing and following longer proofs or arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop precision in written and oral presentation using the language of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should help students to develop precision in both written and oral presentation. Students should learn to communicate with us and with each other, using the language of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize clear, coherent mathematical exposition appropriate to students' level; provide practice and feedback on mathematical writing and verbal explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop ability to read and use mathematical texts and become independent learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should help students develop the ability to read and use text and other mathematical materials. It should prepare students to become, as much as possible, independent learners, interpreters, and users of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach reading strategies for mathematical texts, use of references and resources, and foster habits of independent learning and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop mathematical power (modes of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should help students develop mathematical power, including the use of specific mathematical modes of thought which are both versatile and powerful, including modeling, abstraction, optimization, logical analysis, inference from data, and use of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly teach and provide practice in core mathematical modes (modeling, abstraction, optimization, logical analysis, data inference, symbolic manipulation) to build transferable cognitive tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classrooms must be communities of practice supporting mathematical sense-making
rubrics_metrics.description: If one hopes for students to achieve the goals specified here... then the communities of practice in which they learn mathematics must reflect and support those ways of thinking. That is, classrooms must be communities in which mathematical sense-making, of the kind we hope to have students develop, is practiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design classroom norms, interactions, and tasks to mirror mathematical practice: collaborative sense-making, use of resources, communication, and legitimate peripheral participation into the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework category: The knowledge base
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge base: what information relevant to the mathematical situation or problem at hand does an individual possess, and how is that information accessed and used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating problem solving, distinguish between what tools/knowledge students have and how they retrieve and deploy them. Consider content, organization, and access mechanisms (catalogue vs. retrieval procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework category: Problem solving strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem solving strategies: the methods and heuristics that individuals use to search for and generate solutions in mathematical tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the repertoire and selection of heuristics (e.g. seeking congruent triangles, drawing auxiliary lines, splitting problems), how students choose strategies, and whether they can adapt strategies across problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework category: Monitoring and control (metacognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring and control: metacognitive processes including active monitoring, regulation, on-line decision-making, and orchestration of cognitive processes in relation to problem-solving goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate students' self-monitoring, planning, error-checking, and strategy selection; consider Flavell's categories of metacognitive knowledge, regulation, and beliefs/affects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework category: Beliefs and affects
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs and affects: learners' beliefs about mathematics and themselves (affective factors) and how these influence performance and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to students' epistemological beliefs, misconceptions, confidence, and emotions, since these shape approaches to problems and willingness to persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework category: Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices: the language, methods, accepted procedures, significant questions, and metamathematical views that constitute mathematical practice in a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider enculturation: students must learn the discourse, accepted methods, and criteria of significance and elegance that characterize mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge inventory component: informal and intuitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal knowledge and intuitions about the domain (e.g., general intuitions about circles and tangents; perceptual biases such as symmetry preferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and leverage students' intuitions while helping them reconcile informal understandings with formal rules of constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge inventory component: facts and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and definitions: declarative knowledge about the domain (statements that may be true or false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess correctness and confidence; incorrect facts or misconceptions are part of the tools students bring and must be identified and addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge inventory component: algorithmic procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic procedures: step-by-step methods which, when applied correctly, are guaranteed to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish algorithmic knowledge from understanding; ensure students know when and why procedures apply, not only how to execute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge inventory component: routine procedures and relevant competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine procedures and relevant competencies: methods likely to work in practice but without formal guarantees; domain-typical proof techniques and problem heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize domain routines (e.g., seek congruent triangles, draw auxiliary lines) and cultivate their use as productive but non-algorithmic problem-solving resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge inventory component: knowledge about rules of discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge about the rules of discourse in the domain: understanding how to present, argue, and validate mathematical claims within disciplinary norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach conventions of mathematical exposition and justification so students can participate in disciplinary conversations and construct acceptable proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess degrees of knowledge (inventory levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of knowledge scale: (a) know nothing about, (b) know of existence but nothing of details, (c) partially recall or suspect the details with little certainty, (d) confidently believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scale when diagnosing student resources for a problem (see Table 1); it helps differentiate between absent knowledge, fragile recall, and confident mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish routine procedures from facts/algorithms (uncertainty of routines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine procedures differ from facts, definitions, and algorithmic procedures in that they are somewhat less cut-and-dried: facts are right or wrong and algorithms guarantee success; routine procedures are likely to work but with no guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing competence, treat routine procedures as heuristics that require judgment and may fail; instruction should develop both their recognition and appropriate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze whether problem omissions stem from metacognition or lack of tools
rubrics_metrics.description: In analyzing problem solving, determine whether a solver failed to pursue particular options because they overlooked them (metacognitive/access issue) or because they didn't know of their existence (knowledge/tool absence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This diagnostic distinction guides instructional intervention: teach retrieval and monitoring strategies if access is the problem; teach the missing concepts or procedures if tools are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for misconceptions and misremembered facts as active resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Students bring misconceptions and misremembered facts to problem situations, and it is essential to understand that those are the tools they work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment and instruction should identify and address misconceptions directly, recognizing their role in guiding student approaches and errors.
